slides.text: In my narrow shop on Glassblower's Lane, the shelves are lined with thousands of tiny crystal phials filled with colored mist. I distill the words people swallowed when they were too afraid to speak them—amber vapor for confessions of love, violet smoke for apologies offered too late, pale silver for goodbyes choked back at bedsides. Uncork a phial in the dark, and the voice you lost speaks itself aloud.

On the anniversary of the northern war, a scarred knight in rusted armor entered my shop. He could not speak; a spear had taken his voice at the Siege of Heron's Ford. From his satchel, he drew a dusty glass bottle sealed with red wax and placed it gently on my counter. Inside swirled a storm of warm, golden light.

I picked it up to appraise the vintage and froze. Etched into the bottom of the glass was my own apprentice mark from seven years ago—the night before the army marched north, when I had been too proud to beg a young squire not to go. He reached across the counter, covered my hand with his gauntleted fingers, and together we pulled the cork.
